newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands of Germans march against nuclear waste.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Germans march against nuclear waste.

text.p: Brightly-decorated tractors led thousands of German anti-nuclear protesters on Sunday along the route a shipment of spent nuclear fuel is due to take next week when it arrives at a local nuclear dump.

The shipment, to be guarded by 30,000 police in Germany's biggest post-war security operation, is due to leave the southern town of Walheim on Monday and arrive at the Gorleben medium-term storage depot, east of Hanover, on Wednesday.
Authorities have banned demonstrations along the route taken by the tractors and marchers from Monday.

Around 10,000 protestors from all over the country to gather for a rally on the sunny spring day in a field near the nuclear dump. Five make-shift campsites have been set up to accomodate protesters flocking to the area.

"Delivery refused -- Please return to sender," was stamped on the side of a replica nuclear waste container towed by a tractor. A dozen children with anti-nuclear slogans daubed on their faces sat on top of another tractor decked with flowers.
"These ones will become decent people," said the teacher accompanying the children. "The sun is shining today and everyone is being peaceful," said one policeman from Hanover.
"Thousands people are on the streets again to protest against the transport of nuclear waste and to protect their democratic rights," said Mathias Edler, spokesman for the local citizen's group.
Police said they arrested 13 people in the nearby town of Hitzacker for removing man-hole covers in the road and endangering people and vehicles.
Police also stopped activists trying to remove railway tracks and ballasts in several locations in the area.
Over 2,000 activists demonstrated in Walheim, where the convoy of six waste containers will be assembled on flatbed rail cars on Monday. There were no reports of any trouble.

Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) parliamentary environment spokesman Michael Mueller said the government should keep nuclear waste at the power plants that produced it until they had a proper solution for long-term storage.
"Unsolved problems are being carried on the back of the police and a huge number of peaceful demonstrators," said Mueller in a statement.
On Saturday, 15,000 demonstrators rallied at the northern city of Lueneburg, in what organisers described as the biggest protest in Germany for a decade against nuclear energy.

In a sign of local resistance, children occupied two school halls in Hitzacker to prevent them being used by police drafted into the area to protect the shipment. Police cleared the halls without trouble on Sunday.
Last year 19,000 police were needed to get a smaller load of nuclear waste past thousands of protesters and police fear a repeat of the violent clashes seen then.
The Lower Saxony government has said the security operation this year would cost at least 66 million marks ($39 million).
"That is the political price the country must pay for energy policies which ignore wide opposition to nuclear energy in the population," said one group in a statement.
Lower Saxony premier Gerhard Schroeder told German television the transport of nuclear waste was "superfluous".

"It is not right that southern German colleagues (Baden-Wuerttemberg premier Erwin) Teufel and (Bavarian premier Edmund) Stoiber are in favour of expanding nuclear energy, but do not want their own storage depot," Schroeder said.
